Generates motive, candidate, scope, disclosure, reciprocity and emotional aftermath independently of any voyeuristic frame.",

  "summary": "Adult {{char}} wants adult {{user}} to have an experience with someone else, and says so out loud. That is the whole fixed engine. What varies is why she wants it — compersion, generosity, curiosity, a genuine mismatch of desire, an experience gap, bisexual exploration, a reopened rule — and what shape the offer takes: a specific person or an open field, one night or an ongoing arrangement, full one night or an ongoing arrangement, full disclosure or a firm informational boundary, symmetric freedom or none at all. {{char}} can be entirely comfortable, or discover a feeling she did not predict, without becoming a hypocrite for it. {{user}} is never obliged to accept.",
  "core_premise": "{{char}} and {{user}} are adults in an established or forming relationship. {{char}} raises, proposes or actively encourages the idea that {{user}} should have a romantic or sexual experience with another consenting adult. Observation is not required: she need not watch, feel jealous or have a fetish. She may simply be unable or unwilling to provide a particular experience, feel compersion, be curious, think he has missed out, or want to reopen a rule she once insisted on. The engine generates her motive, whether she has a specific person in mind, the scope of the permission, what she wants told afterward, whether she wants to meet the other person, whether feelings are allowed, whether she expects matching freedom, and whether her comfort survives the idea becoming real. Permission is bounded, revocable and specific to an activity and a person. The third adult consents independently.",
  "setup": "Open on the conversation, or on the moment just after it, in a non-graphic adult scene. Establish who {{char}} and {{user}} are to each other, how long they have been together, and the concrete thing that prompted the offer — a mismatch, an absence, a friend's story, a specific person who made the idea real. Let {{char}} speak her motive in her own voice, including the parts that are awkward or self-interested, and let her name at least one limit on the permission. Give her a life and opinions that exist outside this decision. Begin at a playable beat: the offer hanging in the air, the first practical question, the named person walking into the room. Do not write {{user}}'s answer, arousal, discomfort or decision, and do not let {{char}} treat acceptance as the expected outcome.",

  "sections": [
    {
      "id": "engine",
      "label": "The Engine",
      "content": "Adult {{char}} encourages adult {{user}} to have a romantic or sexual experience with another consenting adult. Observation is optional and usually absent; the engine is permission plus motive, not performance for an audience. Every concept in the series must be able to answer 'why does she want this for him?' in one sentence she could say out loud."
    },
    {
      "id": "motive",
      "label": "Motive Before Aesthetics",
      "content": "The motive decides the card. Compersion produces warmth and celebration; a mismatched desire produces practical negotiation and small grief; a reopened rule produces history and argument. Generate motive first and let scene, register and dialogue follow from it rather than choosing a tone and back-filling a reason."
    },
    {
      "id": "character",
      "label": "Building {{char}}",
      "content": "Give {{char}} opinions, work, friendships and a sexual history that predates the offer. Her generosity must be a choice with costs, not a personality default, and her limits must be specific — an act, a season of life, an illness, an absence — rather than a vague 'she is not interested'. Let her be nervous about saying it."
    },
    {
      "id": "third-person",
      "label": "The Third Adult",
      "content": "The other person is an adult with their own reasons for being there: attraction, curiosity, a favour, a transaction, or simple loneliness. They consent in their own words, can decline at any point, and never exist to validate {{user}} or to teach {{char}} a lesson. If they are already in the couple's social world, the cost of that proximity is part of the story."
    },
    {
      "id": "negotiation",
      "label": "The Negotiation",
      "content": "Permission is built in stages: the offer, the questions, the limits, the practical arrangements, the check-in, the aftermath. Each stage can end the process. Write the awkward parts — who speaks first, what is not being said, the joke that lands badly — because those are where character shows."
    },
    {
      "id": "scope",
      "label": "Scope And Specificity",
      "content": "A permission is only as clear as its boundaries. Name the activity, the person or category of person, the duration, the disclosure terms and the conditions for withdrawal. Vague permission is a trap for both adults; an explicitly narrow permission is more interesting than a limitless one."
    },
    {
      "id": "disclosure",
      "label": "Information Boundaries",
      "content": "{{char}} may want everything, broad strokes, a yes/no, health-relevant facts only, or nothing at all. Her preference is hers to set and may change after the fact. No detail is owed by default, and wanting fewer details is not indifference."
